newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FOCUS-IMF, Bulgaria may reach preliminary accord.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-IMF, Bulgaria may reach preliminary accord.

text.p: Bulgaria's interim government may reach a preliminary funding agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to help it stabilise its crumbling economy and repay foreign debts, Finance Minister Svetoslav Gavriiski said.
"The (IMF) mission has confirmed that we are able to prepare the documents for a new standby agreement in 10 days, by the end of next week before the mission leaves," Gavriiski told reporters.
IMF negotiators started talks with Bulgaria's interim government on Tuesday, warning tough problems must be solved before they can reach a funding deal.
Speaking after a meeting between the IMF mission and a financial stabilisation council set up by the interim cabinet to speed up reform, Gavriiski said:
"If the IMF board discusses the programme in three weeks, the agreement could be approved by end-March or beginning of April and then immediately we can receive the first tranche," said Gavriiski.
The amount of the funds would depend on the programme and the budget which will be completed until next week, he added.
IMF funding will also depend on loans, other lenders, like the European Union, will be prepared to give after a preliminary agreement with the Fund, said Gavriiski.
An EU mission is expected to arrive in Sofia at the end of next week.
"We hope to have an agreement on a policy statememt by the end of the mission (end-next week)," said IMF mission leader Anne McGuirk.
The policy statement would represent the government's programme on how to solve a grave banking and currency crisis, this year's budget and structural reform plans, she added.
The mission said earlier it was impressed by the interim government's commitment to leading Bulgaria out of its economic crisis and to speeding up market reforms delayed in the past seven years.
The caretaker cabinet appointed three weeks ago, has pledged to speed up privatisation aiming to boost foreign investment, shut down loss-making state companies and liberalise prices and trade rules.
The cabinet plans to sell 16 major state enterprises by end-March. They include chemical giant Himko, three cement plants, a copper smelter and a cosmetics factory among others.
Privatisation proceeds will be used to cover part of domestic debt payments.
Ways to resolve Bulgaria's 1.7 trillion lev domestic debt, seen as a hindrance to successful stabilisation, must also be finalised the end of the mission's work, said Gavriiski.
The handling of the economy by the previous Socialist government threw Bulgaria into chaos.

The currency has fallen by some 300 percent against the dollar since the beginning of the year and economists see February inflation at around 100 percent. Monthly inflation last month was 44 percent.
Bulgaria relies solely on foreign loans to repay $1 billion of foreign debts due this year alone, one third of which is due in the first quarter.
Gavriiski said, the cabinet will seek to roll over debt payments owed to the Paris Club of official creditors this year.
The IMF is expected to set arrangements for a currency board system, proposed last year to halt the slump of the lev currency and restore confidence in its crumbling financial system.

The system would require levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank, thus preventing the printing of money.
The programme will also contain legal amendments to bank laws designed jointly with the IMF to enable the introduction of the currency board, said Gavriiski.
The amendments would need to be passed by the new parliament before the currency board is introduced.

In the beginning of February President Petar Stoyanov mediated a deal providing for an early general election on April 19, dissolved parliament and named a caretaker cabinet. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
